strengths: Addresses an extremely challenging and highly practical task: snapshot hyperspectral reconstruction from a single filterless grayscale image and a single phase-only flat lens.

Proposes a well-designed patch-based diffusion framework that addresses key challenges like spatial information leakage across patches and scale ambiguity via a novel physical PSF guidance and dynamic least-squares patch scaling.
Excellent experimental results, showing a substantial improvement (+2.86 dB PSNR) over existing state-of-the-art spectral reconstruction baselines on the simulated ARAD1K dataset.
Strong generalization capability demonstrated on out-of-distribution datasets (ICVL, Harvard, CAVE) without any fine-tuning, alongside useful per-pixel uncertainty estimation.
Thorough optical design exploration and insightful interpretability analysis using perturbation-based saliency maps, revealing that the model implicitly learns the physical forward model.
weaknesses: The evaluation is entirely based on simulation. While the physical simulation is highly detailed, a physical hardware demonstration would significantly strengthen the paper and confirm real-world feasibility under unmodeled optical aberrations and sensor noise.

The guided diffusion sampling incurs a high computational cost during inference due to iterative backpropagation through the forward measurement operator, taking over 20 seconds for a small 256x256 image, which limits its applicability for real-time snapshot imaging.

The paper lacks detailed discussion on how the linear least-squares problem for the per-patch scale factor ($c^p$) is solved, specifically regarding its scalability and computational complexity when scaling to very high-resolution images with a large number of patches.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly challenging and novel task: reconstructing a full hyperspectral image (31 channels) from a single grayscale snapshot captured via a single diffractive flat lens, which offers a highly compact and light-efficient camera design.

The proposed method cleverly combines patch-based conditional diffusion (which requires less training data and scales to arbitrary image resolutions) with a physics-based global PSF-guidance during sampling. This successfully resolves scale ambiguities and boundary artifacts caused by large blur kernels.

A thorough and interesting study on optical design is provided, evaluating eight different point-spread functions (PSFs) to understand how spatial-spectral coding/mixing affects hyperspectral reconstruction.

The method demonstrates outstanding performance compared to several state-of-the-art deep learning baselines, outperforming the next-best method by 2.86 dB PSNR in the grayscale-to-hyperspectral task.
The patch-based formulation shows impressive zero-shot generalization capabilities across different datasets (such as ICVL, Harvard, and CAVE) and higher resolutions without fine-tuning.
The framework provides highly reliable, per-pixel uncertainty estimates that correlate strongly with the actual reconstruction error.
weaknesses: The evaluation is conducted entirely in simulation. While the wave-optics simulation of the metalenses and PSFs is rigorous, a real-world physical prototype and experimental verification are missing, leaving open questions about the impact of manufacturing tolerances and alignment errors.

The reconstruction process is computationally heavy due to the iterative diffusion sampling and the multi-step gradient descent guidance loop. As shown in Table 4, reconstructing a small 256x256 image takes over 20 seconds on a high-end GPU, which limits its applicability to real-time or resource-constrained scenarios.

The global guidance step is highly dependent on having an extremely accurate forward model (the PSF). Discrepancies between the simulated PSF used in guidance and the physical PSF (due to lens fabrication defects) might cause significant reconstruction degradation in practice.

strengths: Highly ambitious and minimalist snapshot hyperspectral imaging setting (reconstructing 31 spectral bands from a single grayscale measurement using only a single phase-only lens).
Well-conceived methodology that elegantly addresses the patch-level scale ambiguity (caused by patch normalization) by solving a least-squares problem during global physical guidance.
Excellent performance in simulation, significantly outperforming multiple state-of-the-art baselines on the ARAD1K dataset (by nearly 3 dB in PSNR).
Strong generalization capabilities demonstrated across several diverse, high-resolution datasets (ICVL, Harvard, and CAVE) without any fine-tuning.
Thorough analysis of optical encoders (comparing 8 different PSF designs), perturbation-based interpretability, and detailed supplementary material providing complete configuration details.
weaknesses: Inference time is extremely high due to the iterative nature of the diffusion process coupled with multiple inner-loop guidance steps (taking over 20 seconds for a small 256x256 image), making it impractical for real-world real-time deployment.
The evaluation is purely based on simulated measurements; the paper lacks experimental validation with physical hardware (a real-world metalens and filterless sensor prototype).

The approach assumes a perfectly calibrated, shift-invariant (isoplanatic) point-spread function (PSF). In real setups, single-lens designs suffer from severe spatial variations (field aberrations) and manufacturing tolerances, which could significantly degrade the reconstruction if not explicitly modeled.

strengths: Innovative Algorithmic Contribution: Effectively integrates patch-based diffusion models (which are highly data-efficient and scalable to arbitrary resolutions) with a global physical-consistency guidance strategy at inference. This directly solves the boundary crosstalk and scale ambiguity issues that usually prevent patch-based reconstruction when the system's PSF is comparable to the patch size.

Exceptional Hardware and Experimental Validation: The authors built and calibrated a real-world prototype with a fabricated TiO2 metalens. They elegantly addressed the sim-to-real gap (e.g., geometric misalignment, stray light, and noise mismatches) using spatial-jitter training and LoRA-based parameter-efficient finetuning on only six real scenes.

Superior Performance and Generalizability: The proposed method outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin (nearly 2.9 dB PSNR improvement on ARAD1K). Furthermore, the model generalizes remarkably well across different datasets (ICVL, Harvard, CAVE) and can be easily adapted to other computational imaging systems like CASSI, achieving state-of-the-art results there as well.

Thorough and Honest Analysis: The inclusion of uncertainty quantification (which strongly correlates with reconstruction errors) and the detailed failure-mode analysis on homogeneous regions provide valuable insights and practical utility for downstream tasks.
weaknesses: High Computational Overhead: The inference time is quite slow, requiring around 22 seconds per ARAD1K image and up to 13–52 minutes for larger experimental/high-resolution scenes on an RTX 3090. Although distillation techniques are suggested as a future direction, the current computational footprint limits real-time application.

Dependence on Spatial Texture: As acknowledged in the limitations, the filterless single-lens design relies entirely on local chromatic blur to encode spectral details. Consequently, the reconstruction performance drops significantly in large, spatially homogeneous regions where many-to-one spectral mappings occur.

strengths: Compelling and highly minimalist hardware design that reconstructs a full 31-channel hyperspectral image from a single grayscale snapshot using only a single flat diffractive lens and a filterless panchromatic sensor.

Well-designed and mathematically sound integration of a patch-based conditional diffusion model with a global physical-consistency guidance mechanism, successfully resolving spatial crosstalk and edge ambiguity across patch boundaries.
Clever solution for the intrinsic scale ambiguity introduced by patch-level max-normalization through a closed-form least-squares estimation of the per-patch scale factors during sampling.

Highly rigorous experimental validation that includes extensive comparisons with eight state-of-the-art methods, cross-dataset generalization tests, and successfully applying the same framework to a different optical setup (CASSI).

Outstanding physical realization and validation: the authors fabricated a 3mm TiO2 metasurface prototype, performed meticulous experimental calibration, and bridged the sim-to-real gap using LoRA finetuning on crudely-aligned real captures.
Provides highly useful interpretability analysis (saliency maps that match the physical PSF) and reliable per-pixel uncertainty estimates that correlate strongly with the actual reconstruction error.
weaknesses: High computational cost at reconstruction time: generating a high-resolution hyperspectral image takes up to 52 minutes on an RTX 3090, which restricts the approach to offline-only processing applications.

Inherent physical dependency on scene texture: as discussed in the limitations, the reconstruction quality degrades significantly in spatially homogeneous or low-frequency regions (e.g., large uniform color blocks) because the mapping from measurement to spectrum becomes highly underdetermined.
Lack of global semantic propagation: since patches are denoised in parallel and coupled primarily by the measurement constraint, long-range contextual consistency across the scene is limited.

strengths: Highly compact and elegant computational imaging design: reconstructing 31-channel hyperspectral cubes from a single grayscale snapshot using only a single metalens and a filterless panchromatic sensor.

Well-motivated, novel algorithmic framework (Guided Patch Diffusion) that allows patch-based training (which is highly data-efficient and avoids overfitting on scarce hyperspectral datasets) while resolving spatial boundary crosstalk and scale mismatches via global physical guidance and closed-form patch scaling.

Excellent real-world validation with a fully fabricated TiO2 metasurface prototype, rigorous PSF calibration, and a clever alignment-robust LoRA fine-tuning method to effectively bridge the sim-to-real gap.

Thorough experimental evaluations across multiple natural scene datasets (ARAD1K, ICVL, Harvard, CAVE) and imaging architectures (such as CASSI in the supplementary), demonstrating clear state-of-the-art performance (+2.86 dB over the best baseline in simulation).
Provides highly useful, well-calibrated per-pixel uncertainty maps that correlate strongly with actual reconstruction errors, which is a rare and valuable feature for computational imaging systems.
weaknesses: High computational complexity during inference: guided sampling requires multiple iterations at each denoising step, making reconstruction slow (up to 52 minutes for a high-resolution scene on an RTX 3090 GPU), which restricts its applicability for real-time scenarios.

Intrinsic physical dependency on texture: as the optical encoder relies on spatial-spectral multiplexing via PSF blur, the reconstruction performance drops significantly in textureless or spatially homogeneous regions.
